sentences.text: Scaniacypselus possessed broader wings than modern swifts and hindlimbs adapted for perching on tree branches. The type species S. wardi had a short, stout humerus and a relatively short, slender ulna. In contrast, S. szarskii featured a longer ulna and a shorter carpometacarpus. The tarsometatarsus was highly reduced but resembled that of treeswifts more than modern swifts. Its feet were anisodactyl, with three toes facing forward and one backward. The tail feathers were only lightly forked.
Many well-preserved specimens of Scaniacypselus with preserved plumage were found in the Messel Pit near Darmstadt, Germany.
The first remains were recovered by D.J. Ward from the Røsnæs Clay in Denmark. The type species S. wardi is known only from a single, almost complete left wing specimen.

The species S. szarskii was originally described by Peters in 1985 as a species of Aegialornis from the Messel Pit in Germany. Mayr and Peters transferred S. szarskii to the genus Scaniacypselus in 2001 based on an additional specimen.

The genus name Scaniacypselus combines the Latin name of the region where the type species was found with the old name Cypselus for the common swift. Mayr classified Scaniacypselus as a basal member of the family Apodidae rather than the subfamily Apodinae.
Scaniacypselus lived during the Eocene epoch in Denmark, Germany, and France. Unlike highly aerial true swifts, Scaniacypselus lived a much less airborne life.
It is debated whether the incision on the sternum of Scaniacypselus has a specific function, as it appears inconsistently across specimens.
